claims.text: Superconductivity in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by electron–phonon coupling modulated by disorder-induced local lattice distortions.
Random arrangement of multiple principal elements creates inherent chemical disorder.
Chemical disorder can be varied while overall composition and electron count remain constant.
Changing chemical disorder changes the extent of local lattice distortion.
Tailored processing parameters can vary chemical disorder without materially changing other relevant sample properties.
X-ray diffraction line broadening and transmission electron microscopy can quantify local lattice distortion.
Increased chemical disorder creates greater local lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortions modify the phonon spectrum.
The distortion-induced phonon-spectrum modification enhances electron–phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling facilitates Cooper-pair formation.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling raises the superconducting transition temperature up to an optimal disorder level.
Disorder beyond the optimum increases electron scattering.
Electron scattering caused by excessive disorder counteracts the beneficial superconducting effect of enhanced electron–phonon coupling.
A moderately distorted sample will have stronger electron–phonon coupling than a minimally distorted baseline of identical composition and electron count.
A moderately distorted sample will have a higher Tc than the minimally distorted baseline.
Samples with excessive disorder may have lower Tc than samples near the optimal disorder level.
The proposed mechanism applies principally to high-entropy alloys whose superconductivity is predominantly mediated by electron–phonon interactions.
Magnetic ordering or strong electron correlations may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Resistivity and magnetic-susceptibility measurements can determine Tc.
A lack of correlation among local distortion, electron–phonon coupling indicators, and Tc across the controlled series would falsify the hypothesis.
